newsitem.title: FRANCE: Airbus crash probe again clears positioning system.
newsitem.headline: Airbus crash probe again clears positioning system.

text.p: Experts investigating the 1992 crash of an Airbus airliner in eastern France have confirmed earlier conclusions that the plane's positioning system was not at fault, judicial sources said on Thursday.
The sources said a report prepared by two court-appointed experts upheld an earlier expert report in the lengthy investigation of the crash in which 87 people died.
They said the experts had re-assembled the aircraft's positioning system in a laboratory and concluded that it had not provided the crew with incorrect data.
Investigating Magistrate Francois Guichard had asked the experts to carry out a new study of the positioning system at the request of lawyers representing crash victims.
The Air Inter narrow-body Airbus A320 was approaching Strasbourg airport on January 20, 1992 when it smashed into Sainte-Odile mountain. Nine of the 96 people on board survived.

"The pilots, at the time of the accident, thought they were lined up for a landing while they were 2.4 km (1.5 miles) off. I cannot believe that this can be considered a normal situation," said Guy-Michel Ney, lawyer for the Echo association representing the crash victims.
Guichard, who is leading the crash probe, said in January he thought the plane's inexperienced pilots were to blame in the disaster.

The initial 1993 accident investigation report ruled out equipment failure and pointed to human error. A subsequent 1994 report modified these conclusions but came up with no firm findings on the cause of the crash.

Airbus planes are made by Airbus Industrie, a consortium made up of French state-owned Aerospatiale, British Aerospace Plc, Daimler-Benz Aerospace, a unit of Daimler-Benz AG, and Construcciones Aeronauticas SA (CASA) of Spain.
